rows.description: A child who stumbles while reading makes a silly face and gets the class laughing with them; the joke keeps control of the moment, though constant clowning can hide worry.

rows.subtype: Memes and GIFs as shared language [Expressing]
rows.description: A teenager replies with a meme or GIF to convey humour, mood or belonging. Context and audience shape meaning, and an in-joke may confuse or hurt outsiders.

rows.subtype: Hiding behind a parent at a party [Actor]
rows.description: A child clings to a parent's leg and refuses to greet anyone; staying away from the scary thing feels like relief, and gentle nearness helps more than pushing.

rows.subtype: Approach: never acting due to fear of rejection [Pitfall]
rows.description: The student rehearses endlessly and never speaks, and after months the crush starts talking with someone else. Avoidance protects from a no but also removes any chance of a yes.

rows.subtype: Baby talk after a new sibling [Actor]
rows.description: A child who was toilet trained and speaking clearly returns to baby talk and clinging after a sibling is born; the child is asking whether there is still room for them to be looked after.
A sick young child may suddenly want a bottle, baby talk or the parent's bed again. Regression during illness is normal and usually fades as the child recovers, without any need for shaming.
A child whose parents respond only to marks feels loved for performance and hides mistakes; the harm is less the standard than the sense that love depends on meeting it.
A teacher or friend sees strong ability going unused and the person turning down chances. Praising effort and progress, not only results, and showing one's own flawed drafts helps loosen the grip.
A child cries harder over losing a marble than he celebrates winning one. Giving up something owned feels heavier than getting an equal thing.

rows.subtype: Approach: go back too early to save belongings [Pitfall]
rows.description: Anxious about a laptop and documents, the person returns to a flooded home against advice. Attachment to things puts life at risk, which shows how loss aversion can override safety.

rows.subtype: Hiding behind a parent at a party [Actor]
rows.description: A child clings to a parent's leg and refuses to greet anyone; staying away from the scary thing feels like relief, and gentle nearness helps more than pushing.
A teenager asks parents again and again whether everything will be fine and checks the same worry many times. Reassurance eases the fear for a few minutes but teaches the mind it cannot cope alone.
